item.content:encoded:
Welcome back to Monday Stat Party, a weekly series showcasing some of the most curious and nostalgia-inducing statistical developments from the past week of Mets baseball. What unites each entry is the sense of intrigue which they aim to spark, and the unbridled love of the game’s anomalies from which they arise. Without further ado, let the stat party begin.
MONDAY
A.J. Ewing hit his 10th home run of the season, giving the Mets 11 players with 10+ homers and setting a new record for most 10-homer players in a season in franchise history (the 2017 team previously held the record with 10 10-homer players). They are now tied for the fifth-most 10-homer players on a team in baseball history, behind the 2019 Yankees (14), 2019 Blue Jays (13), 2018 Yankees (12), and 2023 Twins (12).
TUESDAY
Pete Alonso became the 20th player to record their 300th homer against a team for which they previously played, and the third to do so against a team for which they played 1,000 or more games (along with Willie Horton against the Tigers and Torii Hunter against the Twins). (source: Sarah Langs on X, per Elias Sports Bureau)
Alonso became the second player to hit their 300th homer at Citi Field, as Curtis Granderson reached the milestone with a go-ahead homer in the eighth inning on June 14, 2017, against the Cubs.
The homer marked Alonso’s first game-tying or go-ahead home run while trailing in the ninth inning or later since Game 3 of the 2024 Wild Card Series.
Alonso was actually the second former Met to hit a game-tying or go-ahead home run at Citi Field while trailing in the ninth inning or later. It may not have received the same fanfare as the Polar Bear’s blast, but Adeiny Hecchavarría accomplished the feat with the Braves off Paul Sewald on September 29, 2019 — exactly one day after Alonso set a new MLB rookie record with his 53rd home run of the season. Hechavarría’s homer set up Dom Smith’s memorable walk-off homer on the final pitch of the regular season.
Alonso’s homer snapped Kodai Senga’s streak of seven consecutive saves successfully converted, the fourth-most by a Met to begin their career behind Tug McGraw (15), Anthony Young (12), and Hisanori Takahashi (8).
A.J. Ewing’s second-inning single marked the 100th hit of his career. Ewing and Carson Benge are just the third pair of Mets rookies to record 100 hits in the same season, joining Steve Henderson and Lee Mazzilli in 1977 and Jason Phillips and Ty Wigginton in 2003.
Since 2015, there have been four extra-inning inside-the-park homers in MLB. Three of those four have been hit by an opposing player at Citi Field: Blake Swihart of the Red Sox on August 28, 2015, Daylen Lile of the Nationals on September 20, 2025, and now Coby Mayo of the Orioles on September 15, 2026. The only other extra-inning inside-the-park homer in that span was hit by another Oriole, Austin Hays, on August 11, 2020, at Citizens Bank Park.
Mayo’s inside-the-park homer was a wind-prevented traditional homer, marking the first time a wind-prevented traditional homer has resulted in an inside-the-parker since…Daylen Lile’s on September 20, 2025, at Citi Field. (source: Sarah Langs on X, per Weather Applied Metrics)
The Mets played their 18th extra-inning game of the season, marking the fourth-most in the majors behind the Angels (20), Cubs (19) and Cardinals (19). It’s the most extra-inning games the Mets have played in a season since 2018 (18).
WEDNESDAY
With his 24th stolen base of the season, A.J. Ewing tied Mookie Wilson’s 1981 record for the most stolen bases by a rookie in franchise history.
By allowing homers to Pete Alonso, Christian Encarnacion-Strand, and Jeremiah Jackson, the Mets allowed homers to the same three players in back-to-back games for the first time in franchise history.
The Orioles hit three homers at 106+ mph against the Mets for the second day in a row. Prior to this series, the Mets hadn’t allowed three such homers in a game since April 4, 2023, during a 9-0 loss in Milwaukee.
Chris Bassitt completed six innings at Citi Field for the 16th time since 2022. He is tied with David Peterson for the most six-inning outings at Citi Field during that span, despite the fact that Bassitt played just one season as a Met.
Alonso hit his 125th homer at Citi Field. No other player has more than 80 (Francisco Lindor). It was also Alonso’s 58th homer of a Statcast-projected 410+ feet at Citi Field. No other player has more than 23 (Michael Conforto).
The Mets have now lost five games in a row against the Orioles, and nine of their last 12.
THURSDAY
Nolan McLean has a 0.71 ERA over his first four career starts against the Phillies. That’s tied with Chuck Taylor for the fourth-lowest ERA in a pitcher’s first four starts against the Phillies since the mound was lowered in 1969 (min. 20 IP), behind Rick Honeycutt (0.38), Bob Sykes (0.42), and Hiroki Kuroda (0.68).
McLean recorded his 19th quality start this season, tied with Sonny Gray and Chris Sale for sixth-most in the majors behind Sandy Alcantara (21), Yoshinobu Yamamoto (21), Cristopher Sánchez (21), Cam Schlittler (20), and Michael Wacha (20). McLean is one of only two pitchers since 2015 to reach 19 quality starts in their rookie season, joining Shota Imanaga (19 in 2024). McLean also recorded his 20th start of six or more innings pitched this season, the second-most by a Met in a season since 2020, trailing only Wednesday’s opposing starter: Chris Bassitt (23 in 2022).
McLean recorded his 25th game with at least five strikeouts this season, the most by a Mets pitcher since Jacob deGrom (29) and Noah Syndergaard (27) in 2019.
Aaron Nola made his 33rd career start against the Mets, tied for 25th all-time against the franchise and tied with Randy Wolf and Tim Hudson for second-most since 2000, behind fellow longtime Phillies pitcher Cole Hamels (34). It was his 16th start as a visiting player at Citi Field, moving him into second place behind Gio Gonzalez (18) for most opposing starts in the ballpark’s history.
Nola recorded his seventh scoreless start against the Mets, tying him for the sixth-most all-time behind Rick Reuschel (11), Greg Maddux (10), Juan Marichal (9), Claude Osteen (9), and Jim Bunning (8).
The Mets suffered their 15th shutout loss of the season, tied with the Angels, Guardians, and Pirates for the second-most in MLB behind the Reds (17).
FRIDAY
Juan Soto reached base three times for the 324th time in his career, tying Mike Trout for the fourth-most such games by a player before turning 28 years old. Soto trails only Jimmie Foxx (348), Mickey Mantle (344), and Mel Ott (341).
Soto ripped two extra-base hits with an exit velocity of 108 mph or higher in the same game. In the statcast era (since 2015), a Mets left-handed hitter has accomplished that feat only 12 times: Robinson Cano, Lucas Duda, and Daniel Vogelbach each did it once, Brandon Nimmo did it twice, Michael Conforto did it three times, and Juan Soto has now done it four times in just two seasons.
Zac Thornton recorded his eighth quality start through 14 career games, marking the third-most by a Mets left-handed pitcher behind Steven Matz (10) and Sid Fernandez (9).
SATURDAY
Carson Benge’s eighth-inning single marked his 156th hit of the season, passing Pete Alonso to set the franchise’s new rookie hits record.
Benge recorded his 12th three-hit game of the season, marking another record for a Mets rookie, while notching three hits and a homer against the Phillies. The Mets outfielder with the most such games against the Phillies? Carlos Beltrán (7 times), who had his number retired in a pregame ceremony on Saturday.
The Mets scored 10 or more runs for the 18th time this season, tied with 1997 for the third-most such games in a season in franchise history. The 2000 (24) and 1999 (20) teams are the only ones in franchise history with more double-digit scoring performances.
SUNDAY
Francisco Alvarez’s second-inning single was his 23rd batted ball at 108 mph or higher this season, tied with Juan Soto for the most on the team.
The Mets scored two or fewer runs through nine innings for the 62nd time this season. That’s the most such games for the Mets in a season since 2013 (63), and their second-most in the Wild Card Era (since 1995).
The Mets finished the season with a losing record (3-4) against the Phillies at Citi Field for the first time since 2019, when they went 4-5.
The Mets finished the season with a 36-45 record at Citi Field, their worst in a full season since 2013, when they went 33-48.
Miscellaneous Mets stat of the week:
Here is a list of every player to record 99+ homers and 99+ stolen bases with multiple franchises:
Barry Bonds (Pirates and Giants)
Alex Rodriguez (Mariners and Yankees)
Carlos Beltrán (Royals and Mets)
Francisco Lindor (Guardians and Mets)
Beltrán’s 70.0 career bWAR ranks second all-time among players born in Puerto Rico, trailing only that of Roberto Clemente (95.0). Beltrán won the Roberto Clemente Award in 2013, and Francisco Lindor (who ranks fifth on the leaderboard with 57.2 bWAR) was named the Mets’ 2026 nominee last Monday.
Bonus Stat: There are 32 entries in this edition of Monday Stat Party — one for each year of Mets baseball that Howie Rose has called from the broadcast booth.

item.content:encoded:
New York Yankees fans are frustrated. It's been 17 long years since they've enjoyed a parade down the Canyon of Heroes following a World Series victory. The man primarily responsible for that frustration is general manager Brian Cashman.
If you ask veteran MLB insider Ken Rosenthal, though, Cashman is doing a bang-up job. Rosenthal gushed about Cashman during a recent appearance on Foul Territory.
"It's time, it's past time, to understand what [Brian] Cashman has accomplished," Rosenthal said. "And all of those years finishing above .500, since 1998, yes, they have had financial advantages, too. So have a lot of other teams. No other team has had a winning record every year.
"Now I know, certain fans, certain Yankees fans, will say, 'No World Series title since 2009.' Yes, that is true. It's undeniable, and some of the teams have not been constructed as well as they could've been. I would expect Cashman would say that as well. However, they are always in the mix."
He went on to acknowledge what the standard is in New York - World Series or bust - and he detailed that through line from George Steinbrenner to Derek Jeter to Aaron Judge. But ultimately, his point was that the playoffs are random and that Cashman shouldn't be held accountable for not winning a ring since 2009. Regular season greatness, in Rosenthal's opinion, is a better measuring stick of a GM's abilities.
Sounds ridiculous, right? Even if we grant him that the World Series is tough to win, and it is, that's the point! We're still looking at a clear decline. Think back to the dynasty that began in 1996. The Yankees won four World Series, yes, but they had also lost two others (2001, 2003), meaning that during an eight-year stretch they made it to the final showdown six times. Now consider that since 2009 they only have one World Series appearance to their credit: the 2024 defeat at the hands of the Los Angeles Dodgers.
It's hard not to see a distinct break. Remember, too, that Cashman ascended to the role of general manager on February 3, 1998. He's not fully responsible for those championship clubs, as they had been molded and shaped by Gene Michael and Bob Watson before him.
Also remember that during the 2008-2009 offseason, Cashman's seat was scorching hot, and he was basically mandated by George to go on the huge spending spree that netted New York CC Sabathia, Mark Teixeira, and A.J. Burnett. If his hand hadn't been forced, we likely wouldn't have seen those splashes, and we don't have the ring to show for it.
An honest assessment of Brian Cashman's Yankees tenure pegs him as a middle-of-the-pack general manager
Going back to Rosenthal for a second, he's also been on an apology tour for Cincinnati Reds president of baseball operations, Nick Krall. Krall runs a small-market team, but he enjoys having an MVP-caliber player in Elly De La Cruz, a young ace in Chase Burns, and the likely NL Rookie of the Year in Sal Stewart on pre-arb contracts. That trio makes up just under $2.5 million of Cincinnati's $133 million payroll. He could've set the remaining $130 million on fire and gotten better results.
I bring this up as a reminder that insiders like Rosenthal's sole job is to get inside information and break stories. They get that by cultivating relationships, so when you hear them give an edgy or unconventional opinion, it's because they don't want to hurt a source's feelings.
This isn't to say that Cashman is a bad GM. He's made his share of great moves. He's made blockbuster trades like acquiring Alex Rodriguez, Giancarlo Stanton, and Juan Soto. He's found diamonds in the rough like Brent Headrick (and several others).
But the issue with Cashman is that he doesn't learn from his past mistakes. After failing to acquire prime Johan Santana to protect Phil Hughes, Joba Chamberlain, and Ian Kennedy, he let Ivan Nova, Eduardo Nunez, and Adam Warren stand in the way of trading for Cliff Lee a few years later. Then he compounded the mistake when he failed to sign Lee the following offseason.
In recent years, he's failed to capitalize on Aaron Judge being the literal reincarnation of Babe Ruth by shying away from emptying out the farm to acquire difference makers who would have changed the Yankees' calculus.
It's impossible to look at his missteps and not see titles left on the table. It's criminal that he's enjoyed the best hitter this generation has produced, yet since 2017 has just one World Series appearance to show for it.
Go back to the 1998 team. That should have been his lesson. That club laid waste to the American League, winning 114 games. Entering October, a World Series berth felt inevitable. Going into the World Series against the San Diego Padres, the only question was whether the Yankees would hoist the Commissioner's Trophy after four games or five.
Since those glory days, winning the division is no longer a guarantee. Making the playoffs has sometimes felt like it's on shaky ground. The standard has been lowered, but by the organization, not the fans.

item.content:encoded:
MOOSIC — Edinson Duran became the unlikely answer to a trivia question.
Sunday’s season finale between the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders and Jacksonville Jumbo Shrimp at PNC Field was canceled due to rain and wet grounds. That meant Saturday night’s game was the last one featuring the RailRiders nickname. The team is rebranding and expected to announce the new identity in November.
So when people ask who was the winning pitcher in the final game of the RailRiders era, it isn’t a top prospect like Elmer Rodriguez or an ace like Brendan Beck. It is Duran, a catcher who spent more time on the development list this season than the active roster.
Whenever the RailRiders would need to use a position player to save arms in the bullpen, they would go to Duran. He’s done it eight times in the past two seasons, including six this season.
In the top of the 10th inning Saturday night, Justin Topa struck out the first two batters with the automatic runner on second base. However, with the count 2-1 to Logan Driscoll, Topa reached his pitch limit. With no other options, manager Shelley Duncan called upon Duran. The 24-year old from Venezuela walked Driscoll, then walked Gage Miller to load the bases, but got Johnny Olmstead to fly out to center fielder Duke Ellis to end the inning. The RailRiders won in the bottom of the 10th, 6-5, when automatic runner Yanquiel Fernandez scored from third base on a wild pitch, making Duran the winning pitcher.
“It was really exciting for Duran to come in and do what he did,” RailRiders reliever Eric Reyzelman said. “It’s fun, kind of reminds you why you play this game. Technically, we had nothing on the line playoff-wise. But we did not want to leave this place without a win.”
And so the RailRiders’ final ride has pulled into the station. The team finished 78-68 overall (37-37 first half, 41-31 second half). Its all-time record wound up 1,028 wins and 834 losses.
From the first pitch by Vidal Nuño to Pawtucket’s Brock Holt on April 4, 2013, to the last one Saturday night — Jacksonville’s Stephen Jones’ wild pitch with Kenedy Corona batting — a lot of memorable moments happened in between.
Six times the RailRiders made the playoffs. Three times they lost in the International League championship series (2017, 2018, 2025). But in 2016, they defeated the Gwinnett Braves in four games to capture the IL title, then beat the Pacific Coast League champion El Paso Chihuahuas to claim the Triple-A national championship.
Many notable players have worn a RailRiders uniform.
Hall of Famer Derek Jeter spent seven games on a rehab assignment in early July 2013 while recovering from a broken ankle. During his time here, it became a daily game to see where he was spotted in downtown Scranton.
Later that month, Alex Rodriguez played three games here while coming back from offseason hip surgery. He hit a two-run home run in the second at-bat of his first game.
Curtis Granderson and D.J. LeMahieu were other notable Yankees who rehabbed here over the years. This season, pitchers Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, Carlos Rodon and outfielder Cody Bellinger had rehab stints.
Current Yankees slugger Aaron Judge played 154 games with the RailRiders in 2015 and 2016 and five more games on a rehab assignment in 2019. He totaled 28 home runs and 95 RBIs. Prospects such as Gary Sanchez, Anthony Volpe and George Lombard Jr. spent time here.
“A lot of great players have played for the RailRiders,” said Beck, who wound up leading the International League in earned-run average (2.93), strikeouts (151), innings (135.1), WHIP (1.06) and opponents’ batting average (.210). “To be the last ones to do it is fun. The future is exciting as well. Looking forward to starting something new next year. But to be the team to end the RailRiders dynasty on a comeback win with a good crowd at home is a lot of fun. Definitely a fun day at the office.”
When Duncan played in Scranton/Wilkes-Barre from 2007-09, the team was known as the Yankees. But in his four seasons as manager, the term “RailRiders” has come to mean a lot to him.
“I just always think about the character of every team that I’ve had,” said Duncan, whose record as RailRiders manager is 327-195. “I’ve been lucky to be a part of some good groups that fought all the way to the end. Some good memories and some good relationships. Each year has been a different team and each year has been very special.”
Clint Frazier was a top prospect who played 213 games for the RailRiders from 2016-19 before a severe concussion and lingering symptoms ultimately sidetracked his career. Because of his frequent shuttling between the minors and the majors, he proclaimed himself a “RailRider for Life.”
He made an appearance at Saturday night’s game, signing autographs for fans and throwing out the ceremonial first pitch.
“It was me being a little facetious,” Frazier said. “I think it started around the time I got optioned to the minor leagues in 2019. I was doing relatively well at the big-league level. When I came down here, there was something in the media about September roster expansion and the Yankees were kind of vague on whether I going to be coming back. I remember parking in a parking garage and seeing this sign that said ‘Scranton Life’ and I was like, ‘Dude, I don’t want to be a Yankee. I want to be a RailRider for Life.’ It was a facetious comment and I ended up running with it because it was kind of funny. People obviously took notice to it because I put it on my Twitter bio and it’s been there for like 10 years.”
Frazier was a little surprised and a bit disappointed when he heard the team was rebranding and retiring the RailRiders nickname.
“I’m not a part of the Yankees anymore and I’m not here in Scranton,” Frazier said. “So if they want to rebrand or it’s something the fans want, you give them it. But other than that, I was kind of like, ‘Damn, I guess I won’t be a RailRider anymore. I’ll be whatever they are.’ But I’ll still be a RailRider at heart.”
The nickname has not only meant something to players.
Kristina Knight has been with the team for 20 seasons. She started as an intern with the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre Red Barons, then worked in tickets sales and group sales, sponsor servicing and currently is senior director of partnership management and marketing.
“I think it was extra special because it was a community-thought name,” Knight said. “We surveyed the community and did the poll of submitting your ideas. So I like to think it was the community’s name, which was extra special within itself. The reason we went away from the Yankees name was to give the area more ownership of the team here. I think it did that for sure.
“When we were the Yankees, it was very nice and obviously nice to be included in the Yankees family. But the RailRiders was our very own name and gave our own identity in the minor-league baseball world.”
When the new nickname is announced in November, Knight believes that the community will accept it as well.
“I think it will be as well-received and special to the community,” Knight said. “We are trying to make sure it reflects everything in this area that we find very special and attractive about our area and try to make it a highlight to the nation.”

item.content:encoded:
There hasn't been much for New York Mets fans to get excited about in 2026. But on Friday night, Mets outfielder Juan Soto accomplished a feat that only three other superstars have done in MLB history.
Soto launched a 428-foot three-run blast in New York's 6-3 win over the Philadelphia Phillies on Friday. Despite dealing with injuries this season, the lefty-swinging slugger now has 26 home runs in 103 games. This was also the 27-year-old's 270th homer in the majors. That's noteworthy because the five-time All-Star is now one of just four players to reach 270 home runs and 100 stolen bases before their 28th birthday, according to MLB.com's Sarah Langs.
The other stars on this list include Hall of Famer Ken Griffey Jr. and a pair of three-time MVPs in Alex Rodriguez and Mike Trout. All four players in this exclusive group were playing in the big leagues at 19. And with Soto wrapping up just the second season of his 15-year contract with the Mets, New York fans should get to see the talented outfielder make more history for the foreseeable future.
What's next for Juan Soto and the Mets in 2027?
Heading into the 2026 season, several pundits thought the Mets could compete for the top spot in the National League East. Instead, New York is currently in last place in the NL East at 70-84. But it's not all doom and gloom for the Mets beyond this year's campaign.
In addition to Soto continuing to play like a star while healthy, some of New York's talented prospects have emerged as potential key pieces to the team's future. Starting pitcher Nolan McLean and outfielder Carson Benge should receive some National League Rookie of the Year votes this year, and outfielder A.J. Ewing has turned heads by reaching the majors after starting 2026 at Double-A. The Mets also revamped their farm system at the trade deadline, most notably acquiring the team's new No. 1 prospect, infielder Jefferson Rojas.
New York is expected to be a major spender in the offseason as well. Owner Steve Cohen could make an aggressive offer for left-handed ace Tarik Skubal, while also targeting other top free agents. Either way, with the 2026 season almost in the rearview mirror for the Mets, many fans will be waiting to see if the team can bounce back in 2027.
Justin Binkowski is a lifelong baseball fan returning to cover the sport he loves after spending nearly a decade writing about video games. Before his time as managing editor at Dot Esports, Binkowski attended King's College in Wilkes-Barre, PA, where he was also a relief pitcher on the school's baseball team. While in college, Binkowski was a media relations intern for the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders during the 2014 season.

item.content:encoded:
En esta fecha
Pete Rose llegó a 100 hits por vigésimo segundo año consecutivo; Alex Rodríguez completa el 40-40
Albert Pujols estableció récord de carreras impulsadas para un novato de la Liga Nacional; Mariano Rivera impuso una marca de las Grandes Ligas con su salvamento número 602
1968 — Denny McLain ganó su partido número 31, la mayor cantidad en la Liga Americana desde los 31 de Lefty Grove en 1931. Los Detroit Tigers vencieron a los New York Yankees 6-2, mientras que Mickey Mantle conectó su jonrón número 535 y penúltimo de su carrera.
1972 — César Tovar, de Minnesota, completó el ciclo con un jonrón de dos carreras que le dio la victoria a los Twins en la parte baja de la novena entrada, otorgándoles un triunfo de 5-3 sobre los Texas Rangers.
1973 — Frank Robinson conectó su primer jonrón en el Estadio Arlington, como miembro de los California Angels. Fue el trigésimo segundo estadio de las Grandes Ligas en el que conectó un jonrón.
1984 — Pete Rose alcanzó la marca de 100 hits por vigésimo segundo año consecutivo, un récord histórico. También igualó el récord de la Liga Nacional de dobles con 725, cuando los Rojos de Cincinnati vencieron a los Bravos de Atlanta por 4-2.
1986 — Joe Crowley, de los Chicago White Sox, lanzó un juego sin hits ni carreras para guiar a su equipo a una victoria de 7-1 sobre los California Angels.
1995 — Ken Caminiti, de San Diego, se convirtió en el primer jugador en la historia de las Grandes Ligas en conectar jonrones desde ambos lados del plato tres veces en una temporada, al lograr 4 de 4 con un récord personal de ocho carreras impulsadas en una victoria de 15-4 sobre Colorado.
1998 — Alex Rodríguez, de Seattle, conectó su cuadragésimo jonrón para convertirse en el tercer jugador en la historia del béisbol en conectar 40 jonrones y robar 40 bases en la misma temporada.
2001 — Roger Clemens se convirtió en el primer lanzador en la historia de las Grandes Ligas en lograr un récord de 20-1, llevando a los Yankees de Nueva York a una victoria de 6-3 sobre los Medias Blancas de Chicago.
2001 — Albert Pujols estableció un récord de carreras impulsadas para un novato de la Liga Nacional cuando St. Louis venció a Milwaukee 8-2. Pujols impulsó tres carreras para alcanzar las 120 carreras impulsadas, rompiendo la marca de 119 establecida por Wally Berger en 1930 para los Boston Braves.
2008 — El sistema de repetición instantánea del béisbol produjo su primera anulación cuando un doble de dos carreras de Carlos Peña, de Tampa Bay, se convirtió en un jonrón de tres carreras durante la cuarta entrada contra Minnesota.
2008 — Greg Maddox lanza su entrada número 5.000 contra los Gigantes de San Francisco.
2011 — Mariano Rivera estableció un récord de las Grandes Ligas con su salvamento número 602, sellando la victoria de los Yankees de Nueva York por 6-4 sobre los Mellizos de Minnesota.
2017 — Se establece un nuevo récord de la MLB de la mayor cantidad de jonrones en una temporada, 5,694, cuando Alex Gordon de los Kansas City Royals conecta un jonrón.
2024 — Shohei Ohtani irrumpe en un club completamente nuevo del que es el único miembro: el club 50-50. Hoy, logra su primer partido de seis hits, tres de ellos jonrones, sumando 51 en la temporada. También roba dos bases, alcanzando (e incluso superando) la marca de 50, mientras impulsa diez carreras en la aplastante victoria de los Dodgers sobre los Marlins por 20-4. Hace menos de un mes, se convirtió en el sexto miembro del club 40-40, pero ahora se encuentra solo en este nuevo nivel de excelencia sobrenatural, y de paso, ha establecido un nuevo récord de jonrones en una sola temporada para los Dodgers (superando la marca de Shawn Green).

item.title: [MLB.com] Schlittler, Rice more than just most valuable Yanks, they're indispensable
item.dc:creator: Mike Lupica

item.content:encoded:
The two most valuable Yankees this season are a starting pitcher named Cam Schlittler, from Walpole, Mass., and Northeastern University, a school within walking distance of Fenway Park, and Ben Rice, who comes out of Cohasset, Mass., on the state’s South Shore, about 30 miles from Fenway. If the Yankees are hosting a Wild Card Series against the Red Sox in less than two weeks -- at Yankee Stadium and not Fenway -- Schlittler and Rice will be the biggest reasons.
Schlittler ought to win the AL Cy Young Award and ought to be an MVP candidate for the whole league. David Cone, now a Yankees broadcaster for the YES network and once a great Yankee himself, has one word to describe what he’s seen from Schlittler this season:
“Nails.”
Here’s a breakdown of Schlittler’s ERA, month by month after one start in March, when, of course, he threw a shutout (eight strikeouts) into the sixth inning against the Giants:
1.73 in April
1.48 in May
3.38 in June
1.93 in July
2.33 in August
0.86 so far in September
Carlos Rodón got hurt. Max Fried got hurt. Gerrit Cole joined the season late, and he hasn’t looked like his own Cy Young self lately. It is been Schlittler who has been the Yankees' ace, who is their Game 1 guy, who has carried the staff. He is not going to end up with a 25-3 record and an ERA of 1.74 the way Ron Guidry did nearly 50 years ago. But Schlittler is at 14-6 with a 1.95 ERA going into his last few starts of the regular season. He has been the first young power starter out of the Yankees’ system since Guidry to be this good, and this dominant.
But Rice has been just as important to their offense.
In a season when Aaron Judge was gone for more than 80 games because of a fracture to his rib cage. Then, after Judge finally got back into the lineup and even hit his first home run in months, he left a game against the Twins the other day because of pain in his lower leg. It is why you have to believe, if and when Judge is back in the lineup again, he’s going to be a swing and a prayer the rest of the way.
So No. 99 went away. So did Cody Bellinger, the Yankees’ second-most important hitter a year ago, before he finally returned from the IL. But even when the Yankees struggled to score runs, and even in a roller-coaster year that saw Rice hit just .196 in June and .184 in August, it is Rice who has been the Yankees' hitting star, coming into a weekend series against the Diamondbacks with 38 home runs and still with a chance to knock in 100.
Luis García Jr. showed up from the Nationals at the Trade Deadline to give him some backup. Bellinger has been on a heater since coming off the IL, with five homers, 18 RBIs and a .344 average over his last 22 games. But it was Rice around whom the Yankees built what offense they had before all that, while they were staying ahead of the Red Sox and at least maintaining contact with the Rays.
You know how many homegrown Yankees have hit 40 or more home runs in a season in the last 75 years? Two. One was named Mickey Mantle and the other is Judge. There have been other Yankees sluggers who got to 40 and beyond. Alex Rodriguez once made it all the way to 57. But they all came from somewhere else. Rice is the same as Schlittler: He hasn’t just come to this moment from New England, he’s someone the Yankees drafted in the 12th round of the 2021 Draft (Schlittler was out of the seventh round the following year).
Alfonso Soriano made his own run at 40 more than 20 years ago. Did it twice. But Soriano came to the Yankees as a free agent from Japan. So think about the company Rice will be keeping if does get to 40 homers, starting with his chance this weekend against the Diamondbacks:
Mantle. Judge.
Here is something Rice’s manager, Aaron Boone, has said about him:
"I got my first taste of him in Spring Training of '24, and it was like, 'Oh, OK.' But then this year, it's gone to even another level.”
Here is something else:
“I think he's turning into one of the best hitters in the league."
Rice himself has predictably low-keyed what he’s done for the Yankees so far.
"The year is still in progress, you know?” he said. “It's still going on. We've got more games to play and a long road ahead, so I can't really look back and assess it fully yet."
It really has been a roller-coaster ride occasionally. He has struggled occasionally against left-handed pitchers, but his season-long average against them stands at .254 with 10 home runs and 29 RBIs.
We know what Schlittler’s numbers are. Rice’s, though, can get a little lost sometimes. But in a year where he’s batted everywhere from leadoff to cleanup, when Judge was gone for more than half the time, he has been indispensable, too. And still has a shot to be a 40-homer guy for the Yankees.

item.content:encoded:
PCA began the day with 9.8 Wins Above Replacement (WAR) according to the formula used at FanGraphs, which is also referred to as fWAR. After a huge, four-hit performance, which included his 42nd home run and 37th stolen base in a 7-3 Cubs win over the Braves, PCA climbed over the 10-WAR line, finishing at 10.1. That is blowing away the field and then some. Shohei Ohtani ranks second in the Majors at 6.8 fWAR, and that includes both his batting and pitching value.
The 3.3-WAR gap between Crow-Armstrong and Ohtani equals the gap between Ohtani and the duo of Jake Bauers and Bryce Harper, who are tied for 60th in MLB. If that holds, it would be the first time in 70 years that there was a 3-fWAR gap between the No. 1 and No. 2 players -- since Mickey Mantle (11.5) finished well ahead of Duke Snider (7.5) in 1956. The only other players in the Modern Era (since 1900) to lead by at least 3 fWAR are Rogers Hornsby (1925, '29) and Babe Ruth (1919, '20, '23, '26).
Now, before we go any further, let’s acknowledge two points:
- WAR can go both up and down, so PCA’s might theoretically drop back under 10. (He already did once, after briefly getting to exactly 10.0.)
- There are two major versions of WAR, one at FanGraphs and one at Baseball-Reference (also referred to as bWAR). These systems use somewhat different inputs and calculate WAR differently, so while they generally are in the same ballpark, they don’t line up exactly. In Crow-Armstrong’s case, he still leads the Majors in bWAR, but with “only” 9.3 entering Tuesday, or 1.7 ahead of Phillies pitcher Cristopher Sánchez.
A 10-WAR season by both models is still in play for Crow-Armstrong, if hardly guaranteed, with 11 games remaining. But even reaching that plateau via one of the two systems is quite an accomplishment. For PCA, it comes down to being great across the board. (All numbers via FanGraphs, entering Tuesday.)
- His 157 wRC+ (compared to the park-adjusted league average of 100) ranks second in the Majors among qualifiers, behind only Yordan Alvarez.
- His 6.9 baserunning runs above average, which factors in both his stolen bases and general success on the bases, ranks fifth in MLB.
- Because he plays a difficult, up-the-middle position and excels at it, his defensive value is the best in baseball, edging out Royals shortstop Bobby Witt Jr.
While PCA’s final total will be decided between now and Sept. 27, let’s take a closer look at the company he would be keeping, assuming he maintains his place in the 10-WAR club.
Note: We’re looking at total WAR here, as opposed to just hitting or pitching WAR. Total WAR combines offensive, defensive and pitching value, which affects not just Ohtani, but also pitchers who hit prior to the universal DH or even position players who have made rare pitching appearances.
Players with 10-WAR seasons in the 30-team era (since 1998)
Aaron Judge
2025 (10.0 fWAR), 2024 (11.2 fWAR, 10.9 bWAR), 2022 (11.1 fWAR, 10.8 bWAR)
Judge missed large chunks of 2023 and ‘26 to injury, but he notched 10 WAR via at least one of the two systems in three consecutive full seasons. In each of the three, he posted a wRC+ of over 200, or more than twice the league average.
Bobby Witt Jr.
2024 (10.5 fWAR)
Witt was the epitome of a complete player in 2024. He posted his second straight 30-30 season, led all MLB hitters with a .332 average and 211 hits, had a 170 wRC+, won his first Gold Glove with an AL-best 16 Outs Above Average at shortstop, and finished second in the AL MVP vote.
Mookie Betts
2018 (10.2 fWAR, 10.7 bWAR)
Betts’ 2018 campaign was the peak of a five-year period from 2015-19 in which he averaged 8.1 bWAR per season. He led MLB with a .346 average and .640 slugging percentage, hit 32 homers and had a 185 wRC+ on his way to AL MVP honors with the world champion Red Sox.
Mike Trout
2016 (10.4 bWAR), 2013 (10.1 fWAR), 2012 (10.1 fWAR, 10.5 bWAR)
Peak Trout had many thinking he could end up being the best player of all time, and his three 10 WAR seasons represented the peak of the peak. Those seasons resulted in the 2012 AL Rookie of the Year Award, the 2016 AL MVP and a wRC+ low of 167.
Zack Greinke
2009 (10.4 bWAR)
No pitcher has crossed the 10-WAR threshold since Greinke did so with the Royals in 2009. He pitched to a 2.16 ERA in 33 starts across 229 1/3 innings on his way to his first – and only – career Cy Young Award.
Barry Bonds
2004 (11.9 fWAR, 10.6 bWAR), 2003 (10.2 fWAR), 2002 (12.7 fWAR, 11.7 bWAR), 2001 (12.5 fWAR, 11.8 bWAR)
From 2001-04, a period in which he was named NL MVP each year, Bonds was quite possibly the most feared hitter who ever lived. In ’01, he set the single-season home run record by smashing 73, and from 2002-04, he broke and re-broke the all-time single-season mark for intentional walks -- he set a record with 68 in ’02, then was issued an intentional free pass 61 times in ’03 and an unfathomable 120 times in ’04. Even prior to that historic run, Bonds produced 9-plus WAR four times (1990, ’92, ’93 and ’96).
Alex Rodriguez
2002 (10.0 fWAR), 2000 (10.4 bWAR)
A-Rod had one of the greatest walk years in MLB history in 2000, when he posted a 1.026 OPS with 41 home runs and 132 RBIs for the Mariners just before inking a then-record 10-year, $252 million contract with the Rangers. Two years later, he belted a career-best 57 home runs to go along with an MLB-leading 142 RBIs and 389 total bases for Texas.
Randy Johnson
2002 (10.5 bWAR)
The Hall of Fame left-hander won four consecutive NL Cy Young Awards with the D-backs from 1999 to 2002, averaging 9.5 WAR per season. Johnson was most dominant in the final year of that stretch, going 24-5 with a 2.32 ERA (195 ERA+, or 95% better than league average) and 334 strikeouts in 260 innings.
Sammy Sosa
2001 (10.2 bWAR)
Slammin’ Sammy Sosa won the NL MVP Award behind a 66-home run barrage in 1998. But his best season may have actually occurred three years later. In 2001, Sosa posted a 186 wRC+, or production 86% better than league average, behind 64 home runs and 160 RBIs.
Pedro Martinez
2000 (11.7 bWAR), 1999 (11.6 fWAR)
Martinez was quite good in his first season with the Red Sox in 1998, finishing as the runner-up in AL Cy Young Award voting. But that was just an appetizer for the dominance that followed. Martinez won consecutive Cy Young Awards in 1999 and 2000, each time leading the Majors in ERA and the AL in strikeouts.
Kevin Brown
1998 (10.0 fWAR)
Brown was a workhorse for the Marlins, Padres and Dodgers from 1996-2000, and the ’98 campaign -- his lone season with San Diego -- was his finest over that span. The hard-throwing right-hander finished that season with a 2.38 ERA (2.23 FIP) and 5.2 strikeout-to-walk ratio over 257 innings for the NL champions.

item.content:encoded:
On Monday night, the New York Yankees are playing the first game of their series with the Minnesota Twins at Target Field.
They most recently won two out of three games against the New York Mets (in the Bronx).
UPDATE: The Yankees won 8-3.
Alex Rodriguez’s Former Yankees Teammate Still A Free Agent
With the season nearly over, it’s worth noting that a former Yankees pitcher (who recently became a free agent) is still available.
Chris Martin was released by the Texas Rangers last month.
MLB.com wrote (on August 8): “Texas Rangers released RHP Chris Martin.”
Martin is in the middle of his 11th season pitching at the MLB level.
He had gone 1-1 with a 9.00 ERA in 16 games for the Rangers this year.
Looking At Martin’s Yankees Stint
Martin (who is 40) was picked in the 21st round of the 2005 MLB Draft.
He spent his rookie year (2014) with the Colorado Rockies.
Ahead of the 2015 season, they traded him to the Yankees.
Martin appeared in 24 games for the Yankees that season.
He went 0-2 with a 5.66 ERA.
During that year, Martin got to be teammates with MLB legends such as Alex Rodriguez, Mark Teixeira and CC Sabathia.
Other Stops For Martin
In addition to the Rangers, Rockies and Yankees, Martin has also spent time with the Atlanta Braves, Boston Red Sox, Chicago Cubs and Los Angeles Dodgers.
The 2021 World Series Champion has gone 19-25 with a 3.53 ERA in 434 career games.

item.content:encoded:
Yankees manger Aaron Boone hurts right knee throwing long toss with Aaron Judge
The baseball manager sustained a knee injury during practice; he is currently listed as day to day for his duties
- 1 minuto de lectura'
NEW YORK (AP) — Yankees manager Aaron Boone injured a knee throwing long toss with New York star Aaron Judge.
Boone limped to the podium for his news conferences Sunday and had a soft brace on his right knee. He said the injury occurred during the previous road trip.
“It’s kind of mind boggling,” Boone said after a 2-0 win over the Mets. “I think I hurt it playing long toss with Judgey in Anaheim, but it really didn’t hurt that much, and I’ve been fine and then last night for whatever reason it started hurting me and today it’s killing me. So for now I’m day to day. Today’s not the day.”
The injury is not as serious as Boone's torn ACL in his left knee during a pickup basketball game in January 2004. That injury occurred three months after his homer against Tim Wakefield beat Boston in Game 7 of the AL Championship Series.
New York released Boone and acquired Alex Rodriguez from Texas to play third base.
